title: Battle rules overview
text: VGC battles in Pokemon Champions are Double Battles: each player sends out two Pokemon at once. Each player selects four of the six Pokemon on their team for an individual game. A match continues until one player's four brought Pokemon have all fainted, or the game timer expires, in which case remaining HP percentage and other tiebreakers decide the winner. Matches have a 20-turn limit and each player has roughly 45 seconds per turn.

title: Team construction rules
text: Teams are built from six Pokemon. The Species Clause bans using two Pokemon with the same Pokedex number on one team, even if they are different forms. The Item Clause bans holding duplicate items across the team. All Pokemon are auto-leveled to 50 for battle regardless of their actual level, so EV/IV optimization at level 50 is what matters competitively, not raw level.

title: Regulation sets explained
text: A Regulation Set is layered on top of the base battle and team rules and determines which Pokemon, Mega Evolutions, abilities, moves, and items are legal for a given season. Regulation sets are typically additive: a new regulation usually keeps everything from the previous one and adds new content on top, rather than resetting the legal pool from scratch.

title: Regulation M-A to M-B transition
text: Regulation Set M-A was the first ruleset for Pokemon Champions, running from April 8 to June 17, 2026, and permitted Mega Evolution for a specific list of species. Regulation Set M-B followed on June 17, 2026 and runs through September 2, 2026, covering the 2026 World Championships. M-B keeps the entire M-A roster and rule set intact and adds 22 new base species, 16 new Mega Evolutions across 15 species, and roughly 31 new held items, along with some move and ability tweaks aimed at trimming the most dominant M-A strategies. Nothing was removed from the M-A roster.

title: No restricted or banned Pokemon in M-B
text: As of Regulation M-B, no specific Pokemon are restricted or banned. Any Pokemon transferable into Pokemon Champions via Pokemon HOME is legal to use, including all its available Mega Evolutions, with the Species and Item Clauses being the only limits on team construction. The legal pool sits at roughly 224 base species. A small number of Pokemon such as certain Vivillon and Furfrou forms and Eternal Flower Floette remain HOME-transfer exclusive and cannot currently be obtained in-game directly.

title: Ranked ladder tiers
text: The ranked ladder runs through a beginner tutorial tier, several named ball tiers, and finally the Master Ball tier and Champion tier at the top. Within a tier, sub-rank progress can be lost by losing matches, but once a player crosses a full tier threshold (for example from Great Ball into Ultra Ball), they cannot drop back below that tier for the rest of the season, even on a long losing streak.

title: Mega Evolution basics
text: Mega Evolution is a temporary, battle-only transformation available only to specific Pokemon holding their matching Mega Stone. It usually changes stats and can change ability, typing, or both, and reverts at the end of the battle. Only one Pokemon per team may Mega Evolve in a given battle, and it must actually Mega Evolve during that battle to receive any benefit.

title: Terastallization basics
text: Terastallizing changes a Pokemon's type to its Tera Type for the remainder of the battle. It can be used defensively, to gain resistance against an expected attack, or offensively, to gain a same-type-attack-bonus on a move that would not normally receive one. Each Pokemon may Terastallize only once per battle, and the timing of when to use it is a core strategic decision. Common competitive patterns include Tera-ing to a bulky type like Steel to survive a hit, or Tera-ing to Ghost specifically to become immune to an incoming Normal or Fighting-type attack.

title: Trick Room
text: Trick Room is a field effect lasting 5 turns that reverses turn order: slower Pokemon act before faster ones. Teams built around it typically run bulky, hard-hitting, low-Speed attackers, and try to get Trick Room active before the opponent can respond, often using Fake Out or redirection to secure the first turn for the setter. Trick Room teams typically need one or two turns of setup protection before they can fully take over a game.

title: Weather: Rain and Drizzle
text: Rain, most commonly set by the ability Drizzle (found on Pelipper in the current format), boosts Water-type move power and weakens Fire-type moves, and lets the move Thunder bypass its normal accuracy check. Rain teams pair a rain-setter with sweepers that benefit from boosted Water damage or from Speed-doubling abilities like Swift Swim, which several Pokemon newly legal in Regulation M-B carry.

title: Weather: Sun and Drought
text: Sun, set by the ability Drought, boosts Fire-type move power and weakens Water-type moves. It is the direct counter-weather to Rain, since a Drought user switching in can override an active Rain field and reverse the damage boosts in play. Sun teams typically build around a Drought setter and Fire-type or sun-benefiting attackers.

title: Intimidate
text: Intimidate lowers the Attack stat of both opposing Pokemon by one stage the moment the Pokemon with Intimidate enters battle. It is a strong answer to physical attackers and is frequently paired with Fake Out for a turn-one tempo swing, since the combination both weakens incoming physical damage and denies the opponent a turn of action.

title: Fake Out
text: Fake Out is a priority move that always moves first within its priority bracket and causes the target to flinch, but it can only be used on the turn its user enters the battle, and fails on later turns unless the user switches out and back in. It is commonly used to disrupt an opponent's Trick Room setup on the turn it would otherwise go up, or to protect a slower ally on the turn it enters.

title: Wide Guard
text: Wide Guard is a priority move that blocks all moves that target both opposing Pokemon (spread moves, such as Heat Wave, Rock Slide, Make It Rain, or Earthquake) for one turn, protecting the user and its ally without blocking single-target attacks. Certain attackers with the ability Stalwart or Propeller Tail, or moves used by a Pokemon with those abilities, can bypass Wide Guard entirely. Legal Regulation M-B users of Wide Guard include Gallade, Machamp, Conkeldurr, Pelipper, and Swampert.

title: Spread move damage reduction
text: In Double Battles, moves that target both opposing Pokemon at once (spread moves) deal 75% of their normal damage to each target, rather than full damage. This is why single-target moves are often preferred for finishing off a specific Pokemon, while spread moves are typically used to apply pressure to both opponents simultaneously rather than to secure a guaranteed knockout.

title: Redirection: Follow Me and Rage Powder
text: Follow Me and Rage Powder are priority moves that force all single-target attacks made that turn onto the user, protecting a partner attacker or a setup Pokemon so it can act completely unpunished. Rage Powder specifically fails against Grass-type Pokemon, and against any Pokemon holding Safety Goggles or with the ability Overcoat, since these all grant immunity to powder-based moves; Follow Me has no such exception. Both are commonly countered by spread moves, which ignore redirection entirely, or by a Taunt that disables the redirector before it can act.

title: Speed control: Tailwind
text: Tailwind is a Flying-type move that doubles the Speed of every Pokemon on the user's side of the field for 4 turns, including the turn it is used. Unlike Trick Room, Tailwind does not reverse turn order — it simply makes an already-fast team even faster, or lets a mid-Speed team outrun the opponent for its duration. A common counter-strategy is for the opponent to set their own Tailwind, which cancels out the relative Speed advantage since both sides are then doubled.

title: Prankster
text: Prankster grants a Pokemon's status moves (non-damaging moves) plus-one priority, meaning moves like Taunt, Tailwind, screens, or Rage Powder go before most attacking moves even on a slower Pokemon. This makes naturally slow support Pokemon with Prankster surprisingly good at securing key utility effects before the opponent can respond, though Prankster-boosted status moves still fail against Dark-type Pokemon, which are immune to priority status moves specifically.

title: Overview of new content in Regulation M-B
text: Regulation M-B adds 22 new base species and 16 new Mega Evolutions across 15 species (Raichu gets two distinct Mega forms, X and Y) on top of the full Regulation M-A roster. Most of the new species are returning Mega Evolutions that were absent from M-A, including the three Hoenn starters, Mawile, and Metagross, alongside several Mega forms exclusive to Pokemon Champions. Notable new non-Mega species include Gholdengo, Annihilape, and Grimmsnarl.

title: Established Regulation M-A staples still legal in M-B
text: Because Regulation M-B is additive rather than a reset, established Regulation M-A threats remain fully legal and relevant, including Garchomp, Incineroar, Kingambit, Sneasler, Dragonite, Hydreigon, Whimsicott, and Amoonguss. These Pokemon are commonly seen as teammates alongside the new Regulation M-B additions rather than being replaced by them, since the new content adds options on top of an existing, well-established metagame rather than displacing it.

title: Mega Sceptile
text: Mega Sceptile is Grass/Dragon type with the ability Lightning Rod, which redirects single-target Electric moves to it and boosts its Special Attack rather than damaging it. Its stat spread favors Speed and Special Attack (base stats roughly 70/110/75/145/85/145), tying for the fastest Mega in the format. It is a fast special attacker with access to Earth Power, Dragon Pulse, Giga Drain, Leaf Storm, and Vacuum Wave, though it lacks Draco Meteor and has a relatively shallow special movepool overall.

title: Mega Blaziken
text: Mega Blaziken is Fire/Fighting type with the ability Speed Boost, which raises its Speed one stage at the end of every turn it is on the field. This makes it dangerous if it survives even one turn, since its second turn onward it becomes very fast. It is somewhat frail for a Mega, and is often played with Protect on the first turn to stall until Speed Boost triggers. Its stat spread favors Attack and Special Attack (roughly 80/160/80/130/80/100), making it a strong mixed wallbreaker.

title: Mega Swampert
text: Mega Swampert is Water/Ground type with the ability Swift Swim, doubling its Speed in Rain. It is expected to see heavy play on Rain teams paired with a Drizzle setter like Pelipper, since doubling from a base around 70 Speed lets it outrun much of the format while Rain is active. It gained Wave Crash in Regulation M-B, giving it a strong physical Water-type STAB option alongside its existing Ground-type coverage like Earthquake.

title: Mega Mawile
text: Mega Mawile is Steel/Fairy type with the ability Huge Power, which doubles its Attack stat. Its base Attack of 105 becomes an effective 210 after the doubling, making moves like Play Rough and Iron Head hit extremely hard despite an unremarkable listed Attack stat. Its Steel/Fairy typing also gives it strong defensive utility, including resisting Dragon-type attacks and walling some priority Dark-type moves like Sucker Punch from Pokemon such as Kingambit.

title: Mega Metagross
text: Mega Metagross is Steel/Psychic type with the ability Tough Claws, boosting the power of its contact moves. It carries Bullet Punch for priority, a Meteor Mash with a stat-boost chance, and Ice Punch for coverage, making it a strong all-rounder. In Regulation M-B it lost access to Heavy Slam and Knock Off compared to some earlier formats, but remains a top defensive and offensive Steel-type option.

title: Mega Raichu X
text: Mega Raichu X is a physical-leaning Electric-type Mega Evolution introduced in Regulation M-B, using the Raichunite X Mega Stone (which has no effect on Alolan Raichu). Its ability is Electric Surge, setting Electric Terrain on switch-in, which boosts Electric-type move power for grounded Pokemon and prevents grounded Pokemon from falling asleep. Its stat spread favors Attack and defenses over Mega Raichu Y (roughly 60 HP/135 Attack/95 Defense/90 Sp. Attack/95 Sp. Defense/110 Speed), with Volt Tackle as its signature strong physical STAB move, though Volt Tackle causes recoil damage which is a real limitation given its low HP stat.

title: Mega Raichu Y
text: Mega Raichu Y is a special-attacking glass cannon Electric-type Mega Evolution introduced in Regulation M-B, using the Raichunite Y Mega Stone. Its ability is No Guard, which makes all of its own moves hit with 100% accuracy but also makes all incoming attacks against it hit with 100% accuracy as well. Its stat spread favors Special Attack and Speed (roughly 60 HP, base Sp. Attack around 160, base Speed around 130), among the highest special attacking stats of any Mega in the format. Its signature set uses Zap Cannon, a move that normally has only 50% accuracy but becomes fully accurate under No Guard and is guaranteed to paralyze the target on hit; it is weak to Ground-type moves (2x) since it has no secondary typing to offset that weakness.

title: Mega Pyroar
text: Mega Pyroar is a Fire/Normal type Mega Evolution newly added in Regulation M-B, requiring its own dedicated Mega Stone. It adds another Fire-type Mega option to the format, giving Sun-oriented teams an additional attacker to consider alongside more established Fire-types.

title: Mega Eelektross
text: Mega Eelektross is an Electric-type Mega Evolution added in Regulation M-B. Unlike most Eelektross sets, which lean defensive, the Mega form is built to capitalize on its typing and movepool as a more offensively-oriented pick, giving Electric-type teams a new Mega option.

title: Mega Scolipede
text: Mega Scolipede is a Bug/Poison type Mega Evolution added in Regulation M-B. It is generally used as a fast physical attacker or Speed-control support piece, benefiting from the general Mega stat boost on top of Scolipede's already high base Speed.

title: Mega Scrafty
text: Mega Scrafty is a Dark/Fighting type Mega Evolution added in Regulation M-B, giving Scrafty a bulkier, harder-hitting form. It fits into physically defensive cores that also want reliable Fighting and Dark-type coverage against common threats.

title: Mega Malamar
text: Mega Malamar is a Dark/Psychic type Mega Evolution added in Regulation M-B. Its kit centers on stat manipulation moves like Superpower and Topsy-Turvy alongside solid bulk, letting it disrupt an opponent's setup while contributing its own offense.

title: Mega Barbaracle
text: Mega Barbaracle is a Rock/Water type Mega Evolution added in Regulation M-B, requiring its own Mega Stone. It provides a physically-oriented Rock/Water attacker option, filling a niche that had limited strong Mega representation before this regulation.

title: Mega Dragalge
text: Mega Dragalge is a Poison/Dragon type Mega Evolution added in Regulation M-B. It leans into a bulkier special attacking role, using its Poison/Dragon typing to check a range of common attacking types while contributing reliable special damage.

title: Mega Falinks
text: Mega Falinks is a Fighting-type Mega Evolution added in Regulation M-B. It amplifies Falinks' focus on multi-hit and priority-adjacent physical pressure, giving Fighting-type teams another strong physical attacker option.

title: Gholdengo (new in Regulation M-B)
text: Gholdengo is one of the notable new non-Mega species added in Regulation M-B. It is a Steel/Ghost type known for the ability Good as Gold, which grants full immunity to all status moves, including Spore, Taunt, Encore, Thunder Wave, and Rage Powder, and for reliable special attacking power through Make It Rain (a spread move) and Shadow Ball. Its unique typing gives it strong defensive utility against common physical Steel and Ghost-type threats, while remaining vulnerable to strong Fire, Ground, or Dark-type coverage.

title: Annihilape (new in Regulation M-B)
text: Annihilape is one of the notable new non-Mega species added in Regulation M-B. It is a Fighting/Ghost type with the ability Defiant, which raises its Attack sharply when an opponent lowers its stats, making it a strong deterrent against Intimidate users, effectively turning an Intimidate switch-in into a free Attack boost for Annihilape. It combines this with hard-hitting Fighting and Ghost-type STAB moves, including Rage Fist, which grows stronger the more times Annihilape has been hit.

title: Grimmsnarl (new in Regulation M-B)
text: Grimmsnarl is one of the notable new non-Mega species added in Regulation M-B. It is a Dark/Fairy type commonly used as a support piece, providing Light Screen and Reflect through its Prankster-boosted priority, as well as disruption via Taunt and Spore, making it a strong partner for setup-based teams. Its Prankster-boosted Taunt is particularly effective at shutting down enemy Trick Room or redirection setters before they can act, though Prankster priority status moves fail against Dark-type opposing Pokemon.

title: Countering Rain teams
text: Rain teams are weak to Pokemon that remove or override the weather, such as a Drought user setting Sun instead, since Rain does not boost Electric-type damage while many rain sweepers rely on Water-type coverage that Grass-types resist. Strong Grass-type attackers and priority Electric-type moves are both effective answers, since neither is weakened by an active Rain field the way Fire-type moves are.

title: Rain team building notes for Regulation M-B
text: Regulation M-B strengthens Rain teams by adding Mega Swampert, whose Swift Swim doubles its Speed in Rain, to the existing Pelipper-based Drizzle shell. A common core discussed for M-B pairs Pelipper for Drizzle, a Water-type sweeper like Basculegion or Mega Swampert, and support to handle the team's shared weakness to Grass-type coverage and to Fire-types that can switch in and set Sun to cancel the Rain.

title: Countering Trick Room teams
text: Trick Room teams are most vulnerable during their setup turn, so fast Pokemon with Fake Out, Taunt, or priority moves that can disrupt the setter before it acts are valuable answers. Once Trick Room is active, switching in naturally fast Pokemon becomes a liability, since they will act last; teams facing Trick Room often prepare either to prevent the setup entirely or to run their own slow, bulky answers for the duration of the field effect. Setting your own Tailwind does not cancel Trick Room's turn-order reversal, since Trick Room's speed-order inversion still applies on top of any Tailwind-boosted speed values.

title: Countering Fake Out and Intimidate cores
text: A Fake Out plus Intimidate core tries to win the first turn by flinching one target and weakening the Attack of both opposing Pokemon, denying a turn of action and reducing incoming physical damage. Common answers include Pokemon with the ability Inner Focus, which prevents flinching, or Annihilape's Defiant, which turns an Intimidate drop into an Attack boost instead, along with simply prioritizing offense against the Fake Out user so it does not survive to repeat the tactic after switching.

title: Mega Charizard Y team building notes
text: Mega Charizard Y gains the ability Drought on Mega Evolving, setting Sun and boosting Fire-type moves while weakening Water-type moves, making it a strong direct answer to Rain teams since it can override the Rain and swing that matchup. Teams built around it typically include other Sun-benefiting attackers and dedicated answers to Trick Room, since Charizard Y is naturally fast and vulnerable if Trick Room is set against it.

title: Countering Mega Metagross and Mega Mawile
text: Both Mega Metagross and Mega Mawile are Steel-types and share a weakness to strong Fire-type and Fighting-type attacks, which bypass their Steel typing's many resistances. Mega Mawile's Fairy secondary typing also gives it a weakness to Poison and Steel-type coverage moves specifically, while Mega Metagross's Psychic secondary typing makes it weak to Dark and Ghost-type coverage. Priority moves are a poor answer to either, since Mega Metagross's own Bullet Punch and generally high bulk let it survive most priority attacks.

title: Countering Gholdengo
text: Gholdengo's Good as Gold ability blocks all status moves, so disruption through Taunt, Thunder Wave, or spore-based moves will not work on it. Because it is Steel/Ghost typed, strong Fire-type, Ground-type, or Dark-type attacks bypass many of its resistances and are the more reliable way to pressure it, since physical Normal and Fighting-type moves are blocked entirely by its Ghost typing.

title: Countering Mega Raichu Y
text: Mega Raichu Y's No Guard ability is a double-edged sword: while it guarantees its own attacks land, it also means any attack aimed at it will land with 100% accuracy regardless of the attacker's own accuracy stat or evasion-lowering effects on Raichu. With no secondary typing, it takes 2x damage from any Ground-type move, making Ground-type coverage moves or a Ground-type Tera the single most reliable way to remove it before it can fire off its own attack.

title: Redirection as a team-building tool
text: Building a Follow Me or Rage Powder user into a team lets a fragile sweeper or a Trick Room setter act safely on the turn it is most vulnerable, since single-target attacks aimed at either Pokemon get pulled onto the redirector instead. This is countered by opponents using spread moves, which ignore redirection entirely, or a Taunt aimed at the redirector before it can act, so redirection-based teams often also carry Wide Guard or their own Taunt disruption as insurance.

title: Tailwind vs Trick Room speed control
text: Tailwind and Trick Room solve the same underlying problem, controlling who moves first, in opposite ways: Tailwind doubles your own team's Speed for 4 turns, favoring teams that are already moderately fast, while Trick Room fully reverses turn order for 5 turns, favoring teams built around slow, bulky attackers. If both sides set Tailwind, the relative Speed advantage cancels out since both teams are doubled equally; if Trick Room is active, a Tailwind-boosted Speed value is still inverted by Trick Room's ordering, so the two effects do not simply cancel each other the way mirrored Tailwind does.

title: Garchomp
text: Garchomp is the single most-used Pokemon in Regulation M-B. It is Dragon/Ground type with the ability Rough Skin (damages any Pokemon that hits it with a contact move) as its standard option, though some sets run Sand Veil for evasion on Sand teams. Its stat spread favors Attack and Speed (base 108/130/95/80/85/102), making it a fast physical attacker that outspeeds most of the unboosted metagame while still hitting hard. Its signature move is Earthquake, a spread Ground-type attack, backed up by Dragon-type STAB like Outrage or Dragon Claw and coverage options like Stone Edge or Fire Fang. Common held items include Life Orb (for maximum damage output), Choice Scarf (to outrun faster threats and guarantee a KO), Sitrus Berry, or a Roseli Berry to blunt an incoming Fairy-type attack, since Roseli specifically resists Fairy-type moves and Garchomp is otherwise weak to them as a Dragon-type. Garchomp is valued as a flexible physical attacker that fits into almost any team archetype, from the Mega Charizard Y 'Big Six' offense core to slower Sand or Trick Room builds, which is a major reason for its dominant usage rate.

title: Kingambit
text: Kingambit is a Dark/Steel type and one of the format's most-used late-game cleaners. Its ability Supreme Overlord boosts its attacking moves' power based on how many of its teammates have already fainted, making it hit progressively harder as a match goes on, which is why it is typically saved for the back half of a game rather than led with. Its signature move is Sucker Punch, a priority Dark-type attack that only succeeds if the target is about to use a damaging move that turn (see mech_013 on priority mechanics); this makes it a genuine prediction tool rather than a guaranteed KO, since opponents can play around it with Protect, a status move, or a well-timed switch. Common items are Black Glasses (boosting Dark-type move power directly) or Focus Sash (guaranteeing Kingambit survives a hit at full HP so it can guarantee its own Sucker Punch lands afterward). Kingambit's typing gives it a Fighting-type weakness and it is walled defensively by Pokemon like Mega Mawile, whose Steel/Fairy typing resists Sucker Punch outright.

title: Incineroar
text: Incineroar is a Fire/Dark type support and pivot Pokemon with the ability Intimidate (see mech_006), lowering the Attack of both opposing Pokemon on switch-in. Its signature move is Parting Shot, which lowers the target's Attack and Special Attack by one stage each and then switches Incineroar out for a teammate, letting it apply Intimidate-style pressure twice (once on entry, once via Parting Shot) while bringing in a more favorable attacker at no tempo cost. It also commonly carries Fake Out (see mech_007) for a turn-one flinch, making an Incineroar lead into a Fake Out plus Intimidate core in its own right (see strat_004). Because of this support toolkit, Incineroar fits into nearly any team archetype as a pivot and momentum tool rather than a dedicated sweeper, which is a major reason for its consistently high usage across very different team styles in Regulation M-B.

title: Whimsicott
text: Whimsicott is a Grass/Fairy type support Pokemon and the primary speed-control tool behind the format's dominant Mega Charizard Y 'Big Six' archetype (see megaupdate_001 and strat_005). Its ability Prankster (see mech_012) grants its non-damaging moves priority, letting it reliably set Tailwind (see mech_011) before faster threats can react even on a team that is not naturally fast. It commonly holds Focus Sash to guarantee it survives an incoming hit at full HP and still gets to act, which matters specifically against priority moves like Fake Out that would otherwise threaten it before its own Prankster priority resolves. Beyond Tailwind, Whimsicott also functions as a secondary attacker with Fairy Feather or Moonblast and can disrupt opposing setup with Taunt, which is particularly effective at shutting down an opposing Trick Room setter or redirection user before it can act (see strat_003 and mech_010). A fast Prankster user of its own, or simply pressuring Whimsicott out before its first turn resolves, removes the entire speed-control plan behind a team built around it.

title: Basculegion
text: Basculegion is a Water/Ghost type physical attacker commonly used as the endgame cleaner on 'Big Six'-style hyper offense teams (see strat_005). Its signature move is Last Respects, a Ghost-type attack that grows more powerful for every one of the user's own fainted teammates, meaning Basculegion's damage output scales up over the course of a match rather than staying fixed, similar in concept to Kingambit's Supreme Overlord. It commonly holds a Choice Scarf, since being locked into Last Respects is rarely a downside once several teammates have already fainted, or Life Orb for a more flexible set. As a Water/Ghost type it is immune to Normal and Fighting-type attacks via its Ghost typing while also resisting Fire, Water, and Ice via its dual typing, though it remains weak to Grass- and Dark-type coverage moves. Basculegion is typically held back until mid-to-late game specifically to maximize the Last Respects damage boost, rather than being led with.

title: Farigiraf
text: Farigiraf is a Normal/Psychic type support Pokemon valued primarily for its ability Armor Tail, which prevents priority moves from being used against Farigiraf or its ally at all for as long as it is on the field, functioning as an always-on version of the move Quick Guard (see mech_008 for the general Protect-family category). This makes it a strong answer to priority-reliant threats like Kingambit's Sucker Punch or Fake Out leads. It is also flexible on speed control, able to run Trick Room itself or support a Tailwind-based team depending on the build, and its bulky Normal/Psychic typing lets it switch into and threaten Fighting-type attackers reasonably well. Farigiraf appears heavily on the Mega Aerodactyl plus Mega Charizard Y variant of the 'Big Six' archetype that placed both first and second at the 2026 North America International Championships (see strat_005), where its always-on priority immunity protects the team's Mega Evolutions and glass-cannon attackers during the turns they are most vulnerable.

title: Sylveon
text: Sylveon is a Fairy-type support and special attacker with the ability Pixilate, which converts its Normal-type moves into Fairy-type and boosts their power, most notably turning Hyper Voice into a strong spread Fairy-type attack. Its Fairy typing provides a full immunity to Dragon-type moves and resistance to Fighting- and Dark-type attacks, making it a reliable answer to Dragon-type sweepers like rival Garchomp and to Dark-type threats like Kingambit. Sylveon commonly carries support options such as Calm Mind to boost its own special attacking stats over multiple turns, or protective items like Sitrus Berry or an Assault Vest for extra special bulk (see mech_015 on common held items) at the cost of losing access to non-damaging moves. It is typically played as a bulky special attacker and Dragon/Dark answer within a broader team rather than as a standalone sweeper.

title: Archaludon
text: Archaludon is a Steel/Dragon type bulky support and attacker, most notable as the anchor of the format's most repeated three-Pokemon core alongside Pelipper and Mega Swampert on Rain teams (see strat_001 and strat_002). Its Steel/Dragon typing grants a wide range of resistances, including to Fairy-type moves (which would otherwise threaten most Dragon-types) via its Steel secondary typing, making it an unusually safe defensive Dragon-type. It commonly carries Electro Shot, a Special Attack-boosting Electric-type move, alongside Steel and Dragon STAB options, and can run support moves like Body Press or screens depending on the build. Its combination of bulk, useful resistances, and a rain-boosted Electric-type attack (Electro Shot's accuracy is guaranteed in Rain) is why it is one of the defining pieces of the format's Rain archetype rather than a standalone offensive threat.

title: Sinistcha
text: Sinistcha is a Grass/Ghost type support Pokemon and, at various points, the single most-used Pokemon in Regulation M-B, appearing across radically different team archetypes including Mono-Ghost Hyper Offense, Rain Offense, Sand Balance, and Trick Room flex builds. Its Grass/Ghost typing grants immunity to Normal- and Fighting-type moves and resistance to Water, Electric, Grass, and Ground attacks, while its ability Hospitality heals an ally a portion of their max HP the instant Sinistcha switches in, reinforcing its role as the format's premier healing and support glue. As a lead, its two most common turn-one choices are Rage Powder, to redirect single-target spread damage away from a fragile Mega Evolution and guarantee it survives to attack (see mech_010), or Trick Room, to flip turn order in favor of slower, bulkier teammates against an offensive-leaning opposing lead (see mech_003). Because Rage Powder and Trick Room require Sinistcha to act safely on its own entry turn, opponents commonly try to Taunt or otherwise disrupt it before it can resolve either option.

title: Mega Charizard X and Y
text: Charizard has two distinct Mega Evolutions available in Regulation M-B, using different Mega Stones. Mega Charizard Y is Fire/Flying and gains the ability Drought on Mega Evolving, automatically setting Sun and boosting its own Fire-type moves (such as Heat Wave or Flamethrower) while weakening Water-type moves format-wide, making it both a strong attacker and a hard direct counter to Rain teams (see strat_005). Mega Charizard X is Fire/Dragon and instead gains the ability Tough Claws, boosting the power of its contact moves, making it a more purely offensive physical/mixed attacker without the team-wide weather effect; it trades Charizard Y's team-support utility for higher raw individual damage output via moves like Dragon Claw and Flare Blitz. Because a team can only Mega Evolve one Pokemon per battle regardless of how many Mega-capable Pokemon it carries, some teams pack both Charizard Mega Stones as tech options at Team Preview to keep the opponent guessing about which version, and therefore which weather or attacking style, they will actually commit to that game. Mega Charizard Y is by a wide margin the more commonly played of the two due to its central role in the 'Big Six' archetype.

title: Mega Aerodactyl
text: Mega Aerodactyl is a Rock/Flying type Mega Evolution valued primarily for its ability Unnerve, which prevents both opposing Pokemon from consuming their held Berries — including Sitrus Berry recovery — for as long as Aerodactyl remains on the field. This passive disruption frequently swings close damage races that would otherwise fall just short of a KO, since the opponent cannot heal back the HP they would normally recover. Beyond that, Mega Aerodactyl is naturally very fast and commonly carries Tailwind support alongside Rock Slide for spread flinch pressure, making it a strong alternative or complementary Mega alongside Mega Charizard Y. It is a core piece of the Mega Aerodactyl plus Mega Charizard Y 'Big Six' variant, alongside Farigiraf and Focus Sash Kingambit, that took first and second place at the 2026 North America International Championships (see strat_005 and farigiraf_profile).

title: Mega Tyranitar
text: Mega Tyranitar is a Rock/Dark type Mega Evolution and the centerpiece of the format's Sand Balance archetype. Its ability Sand Stream sets a Sandstorm that chips down non-Rock/Ground/Steel-type opponents every turn while also boosting Tyranitar's own Special Defense while the Sandstorm is active. It is notably bulky for an offensive Mega, able to take hits from a wide range of attackers while still hitting hard with Rock- and Dark-type STAB moves such as Rock Slide and Crunch. Sand teams built around Mega Tyranitar tend to play a longer, attrition-based game than the format's faster hyper-offense builds, often pairing it with Sinistcha for healing support to offset the team's own passive Sandstorm chip damage (see sinistcha_profile).

title: Mega Gyarados
text: Mega Gyarados is a Water/Dark type Mega Evolution with the ability Mold Breaker, which lets its moves ignore the target's ability when calculating their effects — for example, bypassing an opposing Pokemon's Intimidate-immune or damage-reducing abilities. It trades Gyarados' base Flying-type secondary typing for Dark-type upon Mega Evolving, which removes its former Electric-type weakness but introduces a weakness to Fairy- and Bug-type moves instead. It is typically played as a bulky physical attacker with strong Water-type STAB, benefiting from Rain support the same way other Water-types do, though it is not itself a rain-setter.

title: Mega Kangaskhan
text: Mega Kangaskhan is a Normal-type Mega Evolution with the signature ability Parental Bond, which causes most of its moves to hit twice in a single turn, with the second hit dealing reduced damage. This effectively doubles its damage output turn over turn compared to a single-hit attacker of similar power, and also means moves with secondary effects (such as a flinch chance) get two independent chances to trigger. It is commonly built as a fast physical attacker using Fake Out (see mech_007) on the turn it enters, benefiting doubly from Parental Bond on the Fake Out itself in some rulesets, followed by hard-hitting Normal-type or coverage STAB moves.

title: Mega Lucario
text: Mega Lucario is a Fighting/Steel type Mega Evolution with the ability Adaptability, which boosts the power of its same-type attack moves beyond the normal same-type-attack-bonus multiplier. Combined with strong Attack and Special Attack stats, this makes its Fighting- and Steel-type STAB moves, such as Close Combat and Meteor Mash, hit exceptionally hard. Its Fighting/Steel typing gives it a notable weakness to Fire-, Fighting-, and Ground-type coverage despite its many resistances, and it is commonly played as a fast wallbreaker (see strat_006 for the general 'wallbreaker' team-building role) that aims to remove bulky answers early in a match before they can wear it down.

title: Mega Gengar
text: Mega Gengar is a Ghost/Poison type Mega Evolution with the ability Shadow Tag, which prevents opposing Pokemon from switching out while Gengar is on the field (with a small number of exceptions, such as other Ghost-type Pokemon). This trapping effect is Mega Gengar's core strategic value: it can lock a specific opposing threat in place and then either set up freely or force a fight it is favored to win, since the trapped Pokemon cannot retreat to a safer matchup. Its Ghost/Poison typing gives it full immunity to Normal- and Fighting-type moves, though it remains fragile defensively overall and is commonly played around dedicated Trick Room or redirection support to protect it on the turn it enters.

title: Mega Alakazam
text: Mega Alakazam is a Psychic-type Mega Evolution with the ability Trace, which copies the ability of an adjacent opposing Pokemon on switch-in, letting it temporarily gain useful abilities like an opponent's Intimidate or Drizzle. It has extremely high Speed and Special Attack but very low physical bulk, making it a classic 'glass cannon' special attacker that aims to outspeed and knock out a target before it can act, rather than trade hits. Because of its fragility, it is commonly protected by redirection support (see mech_010) on the turn it Mega Evolves, or paired with Trick Room-countering speed control so it retains its natural Speed advantage.

title: Mega Gardevoir
text: Mega Gardevoir is a Psychic/Fairy type Mega Evolution with the ability Pixilate, converting its Normal-type moves into Fairy-type and boosting their power, similarly to Sylveon (see sylveon_profile). Its Psychic/Fairy typing and generally bulky special stats make it a strong special attacker and support hybrid, commonly running Trick Room itself or support moves like Follow Me (see mech_010) alongside offensive Psychic- and Fairy-type STAB. Its dual typing gives it a notable weakness to Steel-type coverage and to Ghost-type moves via its Psychic typing, but reliable resistance to Fighting- and Dragon-type attacks.

title: Priority moves and Sucker Punch
text: Priority moves act before or after the normal Speed-based turn order, grouped into priority 'brackets' — for example, Fake Out and Extreme Speed both have positive priority and act before regular moves within the same turn. Sucker Punch (used by Kingambit, see kingambit_profile) is a priority move that only succeeds if the target is about to use a damaging move that same turn; if the target instead uses a status move, Protect, or switches out, Sucker Punch fails outright. This makes Sucker Punch a genuine prediction tool rather than a guaranteed cleanup move, and is why some Kingambit sets run Focus Sash specifically to survive a hit and guarantee a follow-up Sucker Punch lands on the correct read next turn.

title: Common held items in Doubles (Focus Sash, Life Orb, Assault Vest, Choice items, Sitrus Berry)
text: Focus Sash guarantees the holder survives an attack that would otherwise knock it out from full HP, leaving it at 1 HP instead; this is especially valuable on fast, fragile support Pokemon like Whimsicott that need to guarantee they act even against priority moves. Life Orb boosts the power of all of the holder's attacking moves at the cost of recoil damage on each hit, favoring aggressive attackers over long defensive games. Assault Vest boosts a Pokemon's special Defense significantly but prevents it from using any status or non-damaging move, trading flexibility for raw special bulk. Choice Scarf, Choice Band, and Choice Specs each lock the holder into its first selected move until it switches out, in exchange for a 1.5x boost to Speed, physical Attack, or special Attack respectively; Choice Scarf in particular is common on Pokemon with an otherwise clear best move, letting them outrun and pick off threats that would normally out-speed them. Sitrus Berry restores 25% of a Pokemon's max HP once it drops to 50% or below, giving bulkier support Pokemon extra staying power against the spread damage common in Doubles.

title: EVs, natures, and speed tiers (general concept)
text: Every Pokemon in official VGC play is auto-leveled to 50 (see rules_002), which means Effort Values (EVs, up to 508 total across all six stats, 252 max per stat) and a Pokemon's Nature (which boosts one stat by 10% and lowers another by 10%) are what actually separate two copies of the same species from each other competitively, not level. A 'speed tier' refers to the specific Speed stat value a Pokemon reaches after EV and Nature investment, which matters because Doubles turn order is determined by comparing these final Speed values (modified further by field effects like Trick Room or Tailwind). Players commonly build a Pokemon's Speed EVs specifically to reach a value just above a known common threat, so as to move first against it in a neutral matchup, rather than maximizing Speed by default, since points not spent on Speed can instead go toward bulk or offense.

title: Team Preview and lead selection
text: Before a Double Battle begins, both players see all six of the opponent's team during Team Preview and then choose which four Pokemon to bring for that game and, critically, which two to lead with. Lead selection is one of the most consequential decisions in a match: leads set the tone by establishing a field condition immediately (Trick Room, Tailwind, weather), applying immediate pressure (a Fake Out plus Intimidate core, see mech_006 and mech_007), or playing more defensively to scout the opponent's actual set before committing a Mega Evolution. Because both players select leads simultaneously without seeing the opponent's choice, predicting the opponent's likely game plan from their revealed six-Pokemon roster is a core skill, and a mismatched lead selection can put a player behind before the first turn is even played.

title: Sun archetype in Regulation M-B
text: Sun teams are built around a Drought setter, most commonly Mega Charizard Y (see mega_charizard and mech_005), which automatically sets Sun on Mega Evolving and boosts Fire-type moves while weakening Water-type moves for the rest of the battle. Because Charizard Y also anchors the format's dominant 'Big Six' hyper-offense archetype (see strat_005), a dedicated Sun build and 'Big Six' overlap heavily in practice; the distinguishing feature of a more Sun-focused build is leaning further into other sun-benefiting attackers, such as Chlorophyll-boosted Grass-types that gain doubled Speed in Sun, rather than the standard Whimsicott-Tailwind-plus-Fairy-support shell. Sun functions as a hard, direct counter to standard Rain teams, since a Drought setter entering after an active Rain field overrides it outright, flipping the weather war and turning the opposing Rain sweepers' boosted Water-type attacks weak instead.

title: Sand Balance archetype in Regulation M-B
text: Sand Balance is a slower, attrition-focused archetype built around Mega Tyranitar's Sand Stream (see mega_tyranitar), which chips down non-Rock/Ground/Steel-type opponents every turn while boosting Tyranitar's own Special Defense. Sinistcha (see sinistcha_profile) frequently partners with Sand cores as the team's redirector and healer, offsetting the passive Sandstorm damage the team's own non-immune members take each turn. Sand teams generally play a longer game than the format's faster hyper-offense builds, leaning on residual chip damage, bulky Mega Evolutions, and reliable defensive typing to wear an opponent's HP totals down over several turns rather than looking for an immediate knockout, which makes them a natural check to teams that lack their own reliable recovery.

title: Countering Garchomp, Kingambit, and Sylveon specifically
text: Against Garchomp (see garchomp_profile), Ice- and Fairy-type coverage moves and bulky Water- or Grass-types that resist Ground-type attacks are the most reliable answers; note that a Roseli Berry set specifically blunts Fairy-type retaliation, so a player should scout Garchomp's held item across a set before assuming a Fairy-type attack will land cleanly. Against Kingambit (see kingambit_profile), Fighting-type attackers, or any Pokemon fast enough to knock it out before it can click Sucker Punch, reduce its threat significantly; Quick Guard (see mech_008) blocks Sucker Punch outright regardless of prediction, and Mega Mawile's Steel/Fairy typing resists it defensively. Against Sylveon (see sylveon_profile), Poison- and Steel-type coverage moves bypass its Fairy typing's usual resistances, and since it commonly runs Assault Vest rather than a recovery item, sustained pressure over multiple turns is generally more effective than trying to remove it in one hit.

title: Countering the 'Big Six' Mega Charizard Y archetype
text: Because the 'Big Six' archetype (see strat_005) depends on Whimsicott successfully setting Tailwind on turn one (see whimsicott_profile and mech_012), disrupting that specific turn is the single highest-value point of attack: a faster Prankster user with Taunt, or simply enough turn-one pressure to threaten Whimsicott before its Prankster-boosted move resolves, can unravel the team's entire speed-control plan before it starts. Rock- and Water-type attackers that resist Mega Charizard Y's boosted Fire-type STAB are valuable secondary answers, and Dragon-types like rival Garchomp resist its Heat Wave outright. Because the archetype's damage plan leans heavily on spread moves (Heat Wave, Earthquake) to soften both opposing Pokemon before a single-target finisher, Wide Guard (see mech_008) is an effective defensive tool against it specifically, buying a turn to stabilize before Kingambit or Basculegion can clean up weakened targets.
